inline.s: Zheng’s note: Master Xuelang was named Hongen; at thirteen he went with his father to hear the Great Master Wuji expound the rules of the Lotus at Baoen Temple. Wuji was a man of Huaiyin who had fully mastered the cardinal tenets of the Xianshou and Cien schools, both nature and characteristics, so that the lecture halls of the time flourished under him. Gong was then a boy with his hair still down; for ten days he listened with all his ears and would not leave, and at last he cut off his own topknot, begging his father to give him up as the Great Master Wuji’s little novice. Hanshan the Patriarch was just twelve and had but lately left home at Xilin; in those fresh years they were close in spirit, as the chronicle earlier records of going to the Tripitaka Hall to hear the teaching. From this point, though in brotherly closeness, the Patriarch had a mind that stood apart and above. At twenty, while he sat in meditation with the Great Master Yungu at Tianjie, Gong saw how withered and still he was and scolded him for not going to hear Wuji’s lectures, saying, “What use is a village-shrine earth-god?” The Patriarch answered, “The ancients said: when one has penetrated the nature through the ancestral school, looking back at words is like opening a door and the pestle dropping into its socket.” Xuelang said, “If that is so, then you are my elder brother.” At that time Baoen was destroyed by fire from heaven, and the two wept for three days, vowing to restore it. Later the Patriarch went from Mt. Tai to the capital; the palace plans for the temple almost came together but never quite aligned, and though he passed through the eastern and southern seas he never for a moment forgot the affair of Baoen. Gong, seeing the pagoda’s finial leaning awry, went from door to door with his bowl among the great houses of the city, and in three years brought the work to completion. Ah, both of them may be called men who did not fail their word. Zibo in his heart made light of Gong and from time to time spoke slightingly of him, but when the Patriarch told him the circumstances of Gong’s leaving home, he was startled and said he must be Kuiji reborn. Much of the above I heard from Master Yiyu.
O

Master Miaofeng of Puzhou, named Fudeng, went to Putuo on behalf of the Prince of Shanyin to offer incense. Returning through Jianye, the northerner, unaccustomed to the south, took a damp chill and broke out in sores, so he went to the Tianjie monastery and asked for the work-post of latrine-cleaner, meaning only to rest. The Patriarch recognized him from among the clean latrine floor and the bright, spotless latrine lamp, and they pledged a friendship of life and death, vowing to live on the mountain and go on pilgrimage together. Master Miao said, “If you have this resolve, on pilgrimage I will carry your straw sandals, and if we dwell on a mountain I will supply the water and firewood.” Soon after, his sores healed and he left; six years later, when they sought each other out in the capital, it was clear that at that time his official business was unfinished and the karmic occasion still awaited, and so he had shaken out his robe and gone. The chronicle passes over it with the words “for fear of hindering his secret journey.” In the end, with Master Miao, that one word “truth” is enough to cover a hundred thousand buddhas and patriarchs.
O
In Pinggu county of Shuntian prefecture there is a mountain called Miaofeng, and he took his name from the mountain.
Longqing, first year, dīngmǎo ●

When I was twenty-two I especially proposed the Venerable Yungu of Zhonggong as abbot of the temple, to save it from ruin. This was the matter of the fire; the community’s debts came to nearly a thousand in gold, all of them handled by me. The assembly could think of no way to settle them, so I devised a plan and fixed a limit of three years, and paid them all. That year, by a ministry dispatch, this temple established a charity school to teach the monks; they asked me to be the teacher, and the novices who received instruction numbered nearly two hundred, and so I again took up my old studies of the Zuo Commentary and the other masters. (First meeting with the Venerable Yungu of Zhonggong.)

Zheng’s note: this act not only settled the entanglements of one branch of the family, it settled the entanglements of the abbot of the whole temple; worldly dharma and Buddha-dharma together, one great stroke of strategy. He is called the Venerable Zhong to distinguish him from the Great Master Yungu.
Second year, wùchén ●
When I was twenty-three, that year I gave up the temple school and taught again at Gaozuo Temple, because of the burden of my branch of the family.
Third year, jǐsì ● Fourth year, gēngwǔ ●
When I was twenty-five, in both years I answered the invitation to teach at Jinshan.
Fifth year, xīnwèi ●

When I was twenty-six, I traveled with my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En, to Mount Lu. Reaching Nankang, we heard the mountains were much troubled by tigers, and did not dare climb. So we took the wind and went on to Ji’an, and visited Qingyuan; seeing the temple in ruin and the monks all wearing their hair long, I was moved to the resolve to restore it. So I spoke to the authorities, and chose those under forty years of age and shaved them all, gaining more than forty men. In summer, returning from Qingyuan, I set in order my master’s affairs and settled them well. In the eleventh month of winter I set out on a long journey with a single bowl. As I was about to go north, Xuelang stopped me then, fearing I could not endure the bitter cold, and urged me for the time being to keep to Wu and Yue, where there are many fine mountains and waters to delight the eye. I said: “We people cling with habit to soft warmth; only in a place where it cannot be applied is it easily mastered. Wu and Yue are but pillow and mat to me.” So with a single bowl I went far away. (Second meeting with my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En.)

Zheng feels that the Patriarch had earlier made the contemplation of cool ice and snow; suddenly going north, he roused great valor, cast his body into the trial, and had long since seized both man and environment, so that empty space itself dissolved and fell away.
O
The above closes the case of the branch of the family at the temple.
Sixth year, rénshēn ●

When I was twenty-seven, I first came to Yangzhou; heavy snow blocked the way, and sickness came on me. After a long while, begging food in the market, I could not get in at any door. I asked myself why, and quickly examined myself, saying: “It is only that I have two coins of silver in my waist-wrap to rely on.” So when I saw monks and Daoists who had begged in the snow and gotten nothing, I at once invited them all to an eating-house and threw down the silver, and it was all spent in one meal. The next day, going out into the street, I entered one or two doors and was able to call out, and so got food. Then I rejoiced, saying: “My strength is enough to make light of ten thousand bushels.” I inscribed my bowl: “The vessel that makes light of ten thousand bushels,” and named my robe: “The robe that makes light of the whole world.” Then I made an inscription for them, saying: You entrust me with form, I entrust you with mind. So it is that this one body is made sufficient by it, and all things are in truth made light by it. Now I shall trail the sleeve of the long wind and wear the lapel of white clouds. In rising, like the wings of the swan; in idling, like the scales of the hidden dragon. Roaming free through the cosmos, leaving or resting in mountain and forest. Why then display the brilliance of crimson and purple? I take only what frost and snow cannot invade.

Zheng ponders that one passage of the scene where he first set out begging and entered people’s doors — truly it cannot be spoken, it cannot be conceived. Master Yiyu said that the Patriarch was resolved on the northern journey and Gong tried hard to keep him; the Patriarch put him off by going into the city, and then set out through the heavy snow. Gong returned to the temple and wept bitterly for a long time; this is why there should be a poem recalling his elder brother in the Western Hills. Bianrong and Xiaoyan, the two Masters, both spoke words of deep accord. Xiaoyan was a man of Yan, and built a hermitage in Willow Lane of the western city of Yanjing. He was born in rénshēn of Zhengde, so that when the Patriarch met him at twenty-seven, Master Xiao was already sixty-two. He has a Record of Moon-Mind, in two fascicles of the southern collection and two of the northern, a rarity among Chan records. These words of their meeting are line by line the sealing and transmitting of the matter that goes beyond.
O
In that year the karmic occasion of Mt. Tai began.

In the seventh month of autumn that year I reached the capital, with nowhere to set my foot. Begging, I went a whole day without food; toward evening I came to the tea-shed at the Western Peace Granary, where I got one meal, and I put up for the night at the Yijiao Temple by the canal. The next day the Left Cavalry General Lord Wang Boyu, learning that I had come, invited me to stay, because of his friendship with his younger brother, the second Lord Wang Zhongyan. So I was able to lodge there for ten days, and then waited upon the Venerable Zhong, Master Mahākāśyapa, and went with him to the Western Hills to hear the Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Śūraṅgama, and there were verses written in the Western Hills recalling my elder brother. When the lecture period ended, Mahākāśyapa kept me through the winter to hear the Lotus and the Consciousness-Only, and asked the Venerable An, Master of Dharma, to explain for me the three-part syllogism of Buddhist logic. In the eleventh month Master Miaofeng came to see me. The Master had grown a long beard and wore coarse hempen robes. He first announced himself, saying, “A salt merchant has come to call.” When he entered the door the Master at once asked, “Do you still recognize me?” I looked at him closely and, seeing his two eyes, suddenly remembered him as the latrine-cleaner I had known at Tianjie when he was ill, and said: “I recognize you.” The Master said: “I have changed my head and swapped my face.” I said: “The original face is at ease of itself.” We smiled at each other, with no leisure for anything else. He only asked where I was staying, and I said: “Longhua.” The next day he came to greet me, and as we sat at night he asked why his appearance was like this. The Master said: “Because I have long dwelt in the mountains, my hair has grown and is uncut. Just now a donor, His Highness the Prince of Shanyin, is building a Brahma-palace and has commanded me to beg the inner canon, and so I have come.” He asked after me, and I said: “I have come especially to seek the Master, and also to see the capital and pay one visit to a teacher, to cut off the idle thoughts of other days.” The Master said: “Since we parted I have thought of you without a moment’s break, and supposed there was no karmic link between us. Now that you are here by good fortune, I would gladly accompany you begging, and be your outrider to drive off the dogs.” We talked the whole night through; at daybreak, with a smile, we parted. I then went to consult the Great Master Bianrong and bowed to him, begging the Master to give me instruction; the Master said nothing, only gazing straight at me. I consulted Master Xiaoyan, and the Master asked where I had come from. I said: “From the south.” The Master said: “Do you remember the road you came by?” I said: “Once past, and it is done.” The Master said: “Then your coming-place is clear enough.” I bowed, stood in attendance, and begged for instruction, and the Master opened to me a few words on the matter of going beyond. (The Left Cavalry General Lord Wang Boyu and his younger brother Zhongyan; the Venerable Zhong, Master Mahākāśyapa; the Venerable An, Master of Dharma — one meeting each. Third meeting with my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En; second meeting with Master Miaofeng; one meeting with His Highness the Prince of Shanyin; one meeting each with the Great Master Bianrong and Master Xiaoyan. Boyu, named Daokun, styled Nanming, a man of Xin’an, author of the Taihan Collection; his younger brother Zhongyan, named Daoguan, a noted scholar.)

Zheng reflects that on that day the Patriarch came to know Boyu through Zhongyan, and of the two Wangs it was the elder brother who excelled; and came to know Linzhou through Fengzhou, and of the two Wangs it was the younger brother who excelled — in this world how rare are brothers so evenly matched. At the stare and not a single word, where did he place Fengzhou? At the knee and worshipping the old monk, he granted Nanming his place in heaven. Great Lord Wang’s truly great eye and great vow-power brought to fulfillment the great karmic occasion of Mt. Tai and its great merit — a great man indeed. He set out a vegetarian feast and invited both Masters; one seat’s talk was all words of suchness and no word of deceit, words piercing to the very home, words of the world and beyond the world. With whole heart he urged them on the road, adding more and never ceasing; working through mud and water for others, with no thought for himself — for a thousand ages, would any buddha or patriarch not be moved and give thanks? The two Masters set out for Mt. Tai with their faculties pointed at each other, their footing tested and matched. How then the begging and the slow going, the thanks given and the boarding of the carriage — all because Nanming saw it first. The two men were one road; traveling together or going alone, meeting and parting at their own will, none out of order, and everywhere gazing on ancient traces, and by the river’s edge overtaking and sharing one boat. Treading through straw sandals, faster than the post-relay. Their radiant verses, swifter than the odes. King Wu might well review his troops; why should Boyi and Shuqi not block the horses’ path? If he did not meet the Venerable Darun of the Great Thousand, he had already met the First Patriarch of Shaolin. How fine, how startling — the whirlwind laying low the mountains, sealing from afar Caoxi’s non-movement; night and day, birth and death, awakening to the non-duality of Buddha and Confucius. Only a Buddha knows a Buddha, only a patriarch knows a patriarch. Was it Master Miao who sang it forth, and Nanming who drummed it abroad? Wuji, Yungu, Mahākāśyapa, Bianrong, and the Silent One — those five guiding masters, were they not the first voices that roused the spirit and shook awakening? Xiaoyan and Faguang, were they not the stones from other mountains that polished this jade? Entering Shaolin and paying respects to the First Patriarch — was that not the first cause of the robe and bowl that came from the West? Garrisoning at Caoxi and reviving the Sixth Patriarch — was that not the fruit of the flesh-body taking the seat? The Prince of Shanyin offered two hundred in gold, firmly declined and turned over to Master Guang of Funiu — was it to keep him there, or was it for confirmation? Turning over the gold and departing at once — was it for the old promise made to Master Miaofeng at Mt. Tai, or was it the lion and the hidden dragon, refusing the halter and bridle, to make known the workings of the school? The disciple Fuzheng, reading to this point, joins his palms and praises, saying: Rare indeed is the World-Honored One; the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intention, unloosing the pearl-and-jade necklace from his neck, gave it to Avalokiteśvara — that was the yielding of the gold to Master Guang. Prince Nata tore out his bones to return them to his father and flayed his flesh to return it to his mother — that was the taking leave of provision and the declining of support. A mother may cast her son into the river; a son may disregard the care of his parents; yet those with clear eyes call this the ultimate kindness and the ultimate filial piety of a hundred thousand million kalpas.

Seventh month of autumn: hearing that the court was sending someone to Mt. Lao to investigate, the people were all terrified. Before the imperial envoy came, I had earlier gone to the eastern sea to await him, and so it was settled. The envoy said: “The holy will is exceedingly angered; I fear it will be hard to resolve.” I said: “Whether it is hard or easy, all depends on you, the envoy.” At first, because the people of the east had long been without a place of refuge, and because the temple had newly been built, they were all unsettled; now the holy will was angered over the matter of the inner treasury, and the people were all the more alarmed. The envoy then questioned me about the “inner treasury,” and I answered that it was the Sage Mother’s personal provision. The envoy said: “If it is the Sage Mother’s personal provision, then all the more is the crime of having wasted it grave.” Thereupon he memorialized the matter, and the Sage Mother, hearing it, was pleased. Soon after, the envoy took his leave and returned north; I saw him off at the edge of the sea, and he bade me farewell with tears.
O
In Shuntian prefecture, in Ji prefecture, several peaks rise sheer and cut off; it is called Panshan, and also Panlong Mountain. At the summit there is a great rock which moves when it is shaken.

When I was twenty-eight, in the first month of spring I went to visit Wutai, first seeking out the Clear and Cool Record and traveling to trace its sites. Reaching the North Peak, I saw something about Hanshan that was very fine, and so asked where that mountain was; the monk pointed it out, and I delighted in its rare beauty, and silently took it as my name, writing a poem to record it, with the lines “Let others go as they will; / Here for now I shall rest the workings.” Because I could not bear the bitter cold of ice and snow, I could not stay. I went again to the capital and traveled east begging, until I reached Thousand-Image Peak in Panshan, where I saw a monk who did not speak; I too asked nothing, and at once joined him in gathering firewood and drawing water, begging and passing the summer. Sima Wang sent a letter to seek me, saying: “I fear you have become a starveling of the eastern suburbs.” When autumn came, because Ouzhenbo of Lingnan — who several years before had sent me a letter without our ever meeting, and was now a court scholar — was eager to see me, I therefore returned. (One meeting with the Silent Monk; second meeting with Sima Wang Boyu; one meeting with Ouzhenbo of Lingnan, court scholar.)

Zheng, reading the Record of the Famous Mountains, finds that at the Dragon Gate of Wutai there is a mountain which the First Emperor of Qin, when he whipped the stones into a bridge to cross the sea in search of immortals, whipped without moving it, and so it was called Hanshan. Unable to bear the bitter cold of ice and snow — this exactly looks back to the former state of clear cool ice and snow, and to the words with Xuelang about being unable to bear the bitter cold, secretly lodging his meaning there. As for the affair of the Silent Monk, the biography made by Lord Zhuan records it in particular detail. It says: the Master and Miaofeng met again at the Yan capital and agreed to go up to Mt. Wutai together to dwell in stillness. At that time Master Miao had not yet set out to beg the canon for the Prince of Shanyin, and the Master was lodging in the private home of Sima Wang Nanming. After a long while, he went to visit Panshan, and climbing to the summit, beside a stone crag, there was a recluse within, ashen-faced and earth-soiled. The Master bowed, and the man did not respond at all; he asked questions, and the man did not speak. The Master knew him to be no ordinary man, and likewise sat silent with him. After a little, the recluse boiled tea and took only one cup and drank it himself; the Master too took one cup and drank. When the tea was done, the recluse returned the tea-things to their place and sat upright as before; the Master did the same. After a short while, the recluse cooked rice; when the rice was done he set it before the seat, and took only one bowl and one pair of chopsticks and ate; the Master too took one bowl and one pair of chopsticks and ate with him. When the meal was over, again he sat upright as before, and the Master likewise. In the night the recluse went out beyond the crag to walk in meditation, and the Master followed him, only pacing east and west separately. The next day the Master knew to brew tea at tea-time and cook rice at meal-time; the recluse drank and ate with the Master, and at nightfall walked in meditation likewise. So it went for one seven-day period, and only then did the recluse ask the Master: “Where does the benevolent one come from?” The Master said: “From the south.” The recluse said: “What has he come here for?” The Master said: “Especially to seek the recluse.” The recluse said: “The recluse’s face is just so; there is nothing extraordinary.” The Master said: “From the moment I entered the door I had already seen through you.” The recluse laughed and said: “I have dwelt at this crag for more than thirty years, and today for the first time I meet one of the same wind.” He asked the Master to stay, and the Master forgot to return. One night, as the Master walked in meditation, suddenly there came a sound at the crown of his head, a crash like a thunderclap, and mountains, rivers, and the great earth, body, mind, and world, were suddenly and utterly void, a state not to be compared with the ordinary emptiness before one’s eyes. In that emptiness-concentration he remained for about the length of five inches of incense; then he gradually felt body and mind again, gradually felt his feet treading solid ground, and opening his eyes gradually saw mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and all the appearances of environment, return as before. Body and mind were light and quick, and the bliss was beyond all comparison. Lifting his foot as lightly as wind, he returned to the crag, and the recluse said: “Why were you so long at your walking tonight?” The Master told him fully the state he had attained. The recluse said: “That is a state of the form aggregate; it is not the original possession. I have dwelt at this crag for more than thirty years, and except in rain, wind, and snow, every night I walk in meditation in that state; but if one does not cling to it, it will not obscure the original possession.” The Master deeply assented to his words, bowed, and thanked him for the teaching. The Master stayed at Panshan a long while. When Master Miao set out with the canon, he asked Lord Wang where the Master had gone, and the Lord at once sent a messenger up to the summit of Panshan to find him; asking, he was told the Master was in the crag; the messenger saw the Master and told him how eagerly his host Master Miao awaited him. The Master then took his leave of the recluse, and could not bear to part; but what could he do against the old agreement? The recluse saw him off, his tears flying like pearls, and turned back only halfway down the mountain. The Master returned to the capital, and Master Miao and Lord Wang welcomed him, laughing: “Why did you come back so late?” The Master told them fully the karmic occasion at the crag. The Lord said: “If that is so, then our Master’s dwelling on the mountain is already complete.” The Master said: “It is still only a state on the roadside.” The Lord and Master Miao looked at each other and laughed aloud. Ah, such extraordinary manifestations — how many the Patriarch met in his life, beyond the telling of brush and tongue. Even what Lord Zhuan records, the true record of Panshan, runs to six hundred words, and may be called a karmic occasion of the greatest size. The chronicle dismisses it with a single phrase: at Thousand-Image Peak in Panshan a monk did not speak, and they gathered firewood and drew water together, begging and passing the summer — it looks like no more than an ordinary meal of home tea and rice. A wondrous state may be loved, yet he let it go and went on; though it was because of Master Miao’s old agreement, he was also unwilling to be a follower of the Two Vehicles, a man who saves only himself. The merit of Lord Zhuan’s making the biography lies most of all in this one case.

When I was twenty-nine, in spring I traveled in the Western Hills of the capital. At that time the famous men of the age — the two Wangs, the two Wangs, Ouzhenbo of Nanhai — were all gathered at once in the capital, all of them men I had long admired. One day I visited the elder Lord Wang Fengzhou; when we met, because I was young, he made light of me. I bore myself proudly as host and guest, and he at once earnestly instructed me in the method of composing poetry; I stared at him wide-eyed and in the end took my leave without a single word. The Lord was displeased, and spoke of it to his younger brother Linzhou. The next day Linzhou came to visit; at first sight he said: “Last night my elder brother lost one eye.” I said: “Has the Lord got his one eye?” The Lord clasped his hands and said: “The young man has already seen me,” and we laughed aloud together. Returning, he said to his brother: “Elder brother, you have lost to Vimalakīrti.” And so he gave me a poem, with the lines “One may know that Wang Yishao / Yielded to Master Zhi in matters of principle.” One day the second Lord Wang was living with me and we were reading the Zuo Commentary, and he said to me: “Your natural endowment is uncommonly keen, and you have the spirit and bearing of great letters; my elder brother is the literary patriarch of the age — why not take him as your master and make a name for one school?” I laughed and spat, saying: “Save your elder brother’s knee; one day he will bow to this old monk and receive the meaning that came from the West.” The second Lord was much displeased, and going home told the Sima Lord, who said: “It is true; I observe that Master Yin has the bones of the Way, and one day he will enter the chamber of Dahui and Zhongfeng — would he be willing to make so little of himself for the sake of mere letters? I only fear that idle wandering will be his undoing.” One day, seeing a poem I had written on a fan with the second Lord, with the lines “Body and world, the mayfly’s two wings; / Heaven and earth, one hair of a horse,” he showed it to the second Lord and said: “Is this a monk of letters?” Another day he made a special vegetarian feast and invited me and Master Miao to come together. In the midst of the seat, the Lord said to me: “The Chan gate is desolate and fallen, and it is a great grief. I, a young man, hold it earnestly in mind. I observe your bearing: your future attainments will not be small — why waste yourself in idle wandering?” I said: “I, poor in the Way, have come out especially for the sake of the great matter, to visit teachers and friends, and so I go on pilgrimage. Only now I am looking over the men of the age, to be done with the idle thoughts of other days; it is not idle wandering. And I am about to set out.” The Lord said: “That is true. I observe that in these times there is no one fit to be your teacher; and were it not for Miaofeng, you would have no friend.” I said: “Long ago I singled him out from among the crowd and made a pact as fellow practitioners; and so I have come seeking him, and met him here by chance.” The Lord said: “How strange! If you two truly go, I would gladly provide your crossing.” At that time Master Miao had brought back the canon, and so the Sima Lord gave him two sets of travel documents, and also wrote a piece to see me off. One day the Lord hurried me to come, and asked: “Miaofeng has gone; why did you not see him off?” I said: “Let him go slowly.” The Lord said: “I know you do not wish to turn on another’s heel. Yet it is greatly otherwise. The ancients were not ashamed of small matters, but ashamed that their fame should not be spread through the world. I only wish that one day you may accomplish a work of light for the Dharma-gate; why then fuss over so small a matter of going or staying?” I was moved and thanked him, and so resolved to go. At once I went to see Master Miao, who had already loaded the carriage; seeing me arrive, he asked: “Are you going?” I said: “I am going,” and at once mounted the carriage, and without taking leave of a single person I departed. In the eighth month of autumn I crossed the Meng Ferry and saw the place where King Wu reviewed his troops, and there was a poem lamenting it: “A slab of stone, a ruined stele, leaning at the river’s head; / Here in that year the feudal lords once gathered. / The kingly net should reach as far as heaven and earth; / It should flow on unbroken with the Yellow River.” Passing the place where Boyi and Shuqi held back the horses, I lamented: “To cast away the state and leave its glory — the meaning was already deep; / In vain there remains the ancient shrine, its cypresses dense and dark. / The color of Mount Shouyang is as clear as this; / It is still the heart that held back the horses in that year.” Then I entered Shaolin and paid respects to the First Patriarch. At the time the Venerable Master Darun had just entered the temple, and I visited him but did not meet him. Coming out from the mountain, I saw the old city of Luoyang, the Sutra-Burning Terrace, and the White Horse Temple. Then I pursued Master Miao, and in the ninth month reached Hedong, where I met the Prince of Shanyin, and so stayed to pass the winter. At that time the Prefect Lord Chen, with Master Miao and me, was very earnest, and had the Zhongwu Collected Explanations of the Zhao Lun carved; I collated it. Earlier, in the Treatise on the Immutability of Things, the meaning of “the whirlwind lays low the mountains” was not clear to me, and I had long cherished the doubt; now that I came to it, it was still obscure. But when it came to the brahmacharin who left home and returned white-haired, and the neighbor who saw him said, “Is the man of former days still here?” and the brahmacharin said, “I resemble the man of former days, but am not the man of former days” — then I was suddenly and clearly awakened, saying: “Truly, all dharmas are without coming or going.” At once I came down from the meditation platform to bow to the Buddha, and there was no appearance of arising or moving; I lifted the curtain and stood before the steps, and suddenly the wind shook the courtyard trees and flying leaves filled the sky, and there was no appearance of movement at all, and I said: “This is the whirlwind laying low the mountains and yet ever still.” Afterward, going out, I saw the flowing water, and there was no appearance of flowing, and I said: “This is the rivers rushing onward and yet not flowing.” Thereupon the doubt of a lifetime about birth and death melted away like ice. And there was a verse: “Birth and death, day and night; / Water flows, flowers fall. / Today at last I know / The nostrils point downward.” The next day Master Miao saw me and said with delight: “What have you attained?” I said: “Last night I saw two iron oxen by the river fighting and going into the water; to this day there is no news of them.” The Master laughed and said: “I am glad you have the capital to dwell on the mountain.” Before long Shanyin invited the Chan Master Faguang of Niushan to come; I had long admired him, and when we met I was delighted to have him to sit in practice with, and in talk our minds met. I begged instruction, and he opened to me the practice of investigating apart from mind-consciousness and learning beyond the paths of sage and ordinary; I deeply grasped his purport. Whenever I heard the Master discourse, his voice came forth like the sound of a heavenly drum. At that time I knew that one who has awakened and understood the mind-ground indeed speaks and breathes differently, and I deeply submitted to him. One day he searched out my poems from my bag and read them, and sighed: “Such fine lines — where did you get them?” Then he laughed: “Fine they are, but that one opening is still not through.” I said: “Is the Master’s one opening through or not?” The Master said: “Thirty years catching dragons and seizing tigers, and today a rabbit runs out of the grass and gives me a start.” I said: “The Master is no dragon-catching, tiger-seizing hand.” The Master picked up his staff and would have struck me; I at once held it fast, and stroking his beard with my hand said: “You call it a rabbit, when it is plainly a frog.” The Master laughed and let it drop. One day the Master said: “You need not go elsewhere; I would have you dwell with me at Old Funiu — that is my hope.” I said: “Judging by the Master’s Dharma-wit and eloquence, he is not less than Dahui; yet in daily life he seems always to have a madman’s manner, humming and mumbling without a moment’s pause. Why is that?” The Master said: “That is my Chan illness. When I first awakened, verses poured from me like a stream, day and night without cease, and I could not stop them myself, and so it became an illness.” I said: “When this illness first arose, how should it have been treated?” The Master said: “When this illness breaks out, if one cannot see through it oneself, one needs a man of great eye and hand to give one a sound beating and make one sleep soundly; on waking it naturally vanishes. My only regret is that I have no poison hand.” The Master knew that I was to leave for Wutai at the new year, and so sent me off with a poem, with the lines “The lion in the clouds, ride it here to see; / The hidden dragon in the cave, let it go and rest.” He asked: “Do you know?” I said: “I do not.” The Master said: “I would have you not grasp at a dead snake.” I nodded. For long there had been no master-craftsman in the Chan way, and only on meeting Master Guang did I know that the school still has its workings. The Prince of Shanyin, learning that my two parents were living, gave me two hundred in gold as provision for their care in old age. I thanked him, saying: “I, poor in the Way, have only begun my pilgrimage and cannot yet save myself; how should I dare involve my two parents?” I firmly declined and turned it over to Master Guang. (Second meeting with Ouzhenbo of Nanhai; one meeting each with the elder Lord Wang Fengzhou and the second Lord Linzhou. Third meeting with Sima Wang Boyu; second meeting with the second Lord Zhongyan; third meeting with Master Miaofeng; one meeting with the Venerable Master Darun; second meeting with the Prince of Shanyin; one meeting with the Prefect Lord Chen; one meeting with Chan Master Faguang. Fengzhou, named Shizhen, a man of Taicang, an official to the rank of Junior Sima; his younger brother Linzhou, named Shimao, an official to the rank of Grand Minister of Ceremonies.)
O

Zheng further notes that the biography made by Lord Zhuan says: Master Miao accompanied the Master to fetch the sutras, and going from Henan they turned into Shanxi and reached Puzhou. The Prince of Shanyin, hearing that the canon was about to arrive, led all the clan lords with banners, canopies, music, and incense and flowers to welcome the sutras into the palace. Master Miao told the Prince: “The Master Cheng-yin of whom I spoke has also come.” The Prince, hearing it, was overjoyed; he first invited the Master to meet him, and only afterward had the canon enshrined. He kept the Master to dwell in the palace, sitting face to face with him at every hour, searching out the cardinal purport of the Śūraṅgama. The Prince asked Master Miao to request the Master to lecture on the Śūraṅgama Sutra; the Master wept and firmly declined, saying: “I came to dwell on the mountain, not to lecture on sutras,” and at once wished to flee. The Prince, knowing his resolve could not be turned, bowed low and pressed him to stay two or three months, and then charged Master Miao to accompany the Master to dwell on the mountain. Alas, the Patriarch had long since known Master Miao at Tianjie, and Master Miao had long since commended the Patriarch to Shanyin; hence meeting all at once, at first sight they were as old friends. The excellent affair of discoursing on the sutras ended when it should. What is called “in the knowing between people, what is valued is knowing the heart” is just this.
Third year, yǐhài ●

When I was thirty, in the first month I went up to Wutai with Master Miao from Hedong, passing through Pingyang, which was the Master’s home country. The Master, poor from youth, had met a year of famine; his father and mother died, and there were no grave-clothes for burial. At this time Shanyin and one or two of the authorities helped him, and I divined a high, open site for their joint burial, and composed the grave-inscription. The Master’s secular surname was Xu, and his family lived in the eastern quarter of Pingyang, being, it is said, descendants of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period. At that time the Prefect Lord Hu, styled Shun’an, a man of Donglai, heard that I had come and lodged outside the city, wishing to see me once but unable; and when I set out, he sent me post-station credentials. I said: “A man of the Way on pilgrimage has his straw sandals; what use has he for these?” After I had gone, he pursued me and only caught up at Lingshi, and we went together to the provincial capital, where he kept me in talk for several days and sent servants to escort me to Mt. Tai. On the fifteenth day of the second month I lodged at the Tayuan Temple; the host Dafang divined me a dwelling at the Dragon Gate of the North Peak, the most secluded and precipitous place of all. On the third day of the third month, from out of a snowdrift I cleared several rooms of an old house and dwelt there. At the time I saw ten thousand mountains of ice and snow, exactly the realm I had long admired; my body and mind were washed clean, as though I had entered the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Before long Master Miao went off to visit the Night Terrace, and I dwelt here alone, raising one thought only; when people came I did not speak, but only looked at them. After a long time I looked on people as on stumps, until I reached the place of not knowing a single character. At first, when the great wind rose from time to time, ten thousand openings roared with rage; the ice melted and the torrents of the ravines rushed and surged like thunder; and in the stillness I heard sounds like a thousand armies and ten thousand horses marching out — I took it as very noisy and disturbing, and so asked Master Miao. The Master said: “The environment arises from the mind; it does not come from outside.” I heard that an ancient said: “Hear the sound of water for thirty years without turning the root of mind, and you will attest Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration.” So, at a single-plank bridge over the stream, I sat or stood on it every day; at first the sound of the water was distinct, and after long practice the sound was heard when a thought stirred and not heard when none stirred. One day, sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my body, and the sound was utterly still; from then on all noises were still and no longer disturbed me. What I ate each day was only bran mixed with wild greens, and a soup of a little rice to send it down. At first people gave me three pecks of rice, and after half a year there was still some left. One day, after the gruel, as I walked in meditation, I suddenly stood fixed, and saw neither body nor mind, only one great treasury of light, perfect and profoundly still, like a great perfect mirror, in which mountains, rivers, and the great earth appeared as reflections; and when I came to, all was clear, and though I sought body and mind I could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: A single startled thought, and the mad mind rests; Inside and out, sense-roots and dust are all pierced through. Turning over, I shatter the great empty space; The myriad forms, dense and manifold, arise and cease with it. From then on, inside and out were utterly clear, and sounds, forms, and appearances no longer obstructed me; all my former doubts dissolved at once. When I looked at my cooking-pot, it had already grown dusty, and because I was alone with no companion, I did not know how long it had been. That summer Xuelang came north and made a point of seeing me; when he reached Mt. Tai and sat in my room, he could not keep back his grief, and after two nights he took his leave. In winter I built a plank hut to dwell in. (Fourth meeting with Master Miaofeng; third meeting with the Prince of Shanyin; one meeting each with Hu Shun’an, Prefect of Pingyang, and the host Dafang; fourth meeting with Xuelang. Shun’an is the later Grand Censor Hu.)

Zheng, at the Zongjing Hall of the Jingci Temple, heard from the Patriarch’s eminent disciples Zhiwei, Xuzhong, and Xiuliu, the three Masters, that the Great Master and Master Miao were at the Dragon Gate of Mt. Tai, sitting on the Dragon-Flipping Stone listening to the boiling spring; for a whole year, until the sound of the spring was unbroken and yet unheard, he was able to enter concentration. Master Miao, knowing the Great Master was about to enter concentration, made a separate hut at the wooden-tile beam; and when the Great Master entered concentration, no one knew how many days passed before he came out. From this one knows that the dust on the cooking-pot was the affair of his solitary dwelling in concentration. So one knows that without a man of awakening, none can enter concentration; and without a man of austerities, none can awaken. The ancient venerable ones said that great awakening comes eighteen times over, and small awakenings beyond counting. To say that one awakening means no further awakening is a great error. In those years the vow-power took ice and snow and coolness as its contemplation; here the karmic occasion came to fulfillment, and through ice and snow and coolness he gained power. This is what is meant by the fuel exhausted and the fire passed on, what is meant by the transmission of the lamp. The patch-robed monks of today who transmit the lamp are transmitting only the fuel.
O

A few words in direct record of Gong still carry the meaning of that year’s pleading against the bitter cold, never forgetting the bond of shared birth and friendship. Gong’s biography relates that on that day he sought out where the Master Han was, and passing Song and Shao and Funiu, went up to the Dragon Gate of Wutai and found him in the drifts of ice and snow, with his waist-wallet and his bowl of rice, vowing to share life and death. The Master said to him: “Each person has his own resolve, and each his own karmic occasion. Your karmic occasion lies in practicing the Dharma to continue the wisdom-life; you should not grow old in withered stillness. This Way has long been buried in Jiangnan; you should carry on the Dharma-seat of your own master Wuji, shoulder the entrustment, and be the eye for gods and humans, so as not to fail the karmic occasion of leaving the world.” Gong nodded his assent, and so they parted with grave ceremony. Afterward he traveled with his staff through the several commanderies of the Three Wu, and taught the Dharma for thirty years, surrounded by great assemblies, so that the lecture seats of the southeast flourished exceedingly.
O

In Wutai county of Taiyuan prefecture, Shanxi, there is Mount Wutai, whose five peaks rise above the clouds; their tops and backs can all be climbed, and so they are called terraces. It is the dwelling of Mañjuśrī, and is called the Clear and Cool Mountain. Indeed, the Patriarch’s karmic occasion of coolness and ice and snow ran from first to last. That the Tathagata cultivated the Way in the Snow Mountains, and that the patriarchs stood in the snow to receive the transmission — now I believe it.
Fourth year, bǐngzǐ ●

When I was thirty-one, after my awakening, having no one to ask for increase, I opened the Śūraṅgama to seal and confirm it. At first I had never heard this sutra expounded and did not understand its meaning at all, so now I simply illumined it with direct perception. If a thought of mind-consciousness stirred even slightly, I allowed no deliberation. So for eight months, and the purport of the whole sutra was clear beyond doubt. In the third month of spring Master Lianchi visited Wutai and came to call; he stayed ten days, and by night we talked heart to heart with deep accord. In the seventh month of autumn Lord Hu, Prefect of Pingyang, transferred to the Yanping military commission, came into the mountains to visit me; in the quiet room we ate only oats

and wild-herb pickles. At that time it was just then fiercely hot, and his outriders went into the mountain ravine and broke ice to chew; the Lord saw it and said: “This is another world; since I came here, my worldly thoughts have been as cool as this ice.” In the tenth month of winter that year the host of the Tayuan Temple, Dafang, was falsely accused and sued before the circuit office, and it was proposed to send him into exile and return him to lay life, so that the monastery was all but ruined. At that time Master Chekong of Mount Lu came and dwelt with me, and happening to see this affair, found it too bitter. I said: “No harm,” and went myself to Lord Hu, going through heavy snow. When we met, Lord Hu said with delight: “I was just thinking how the heavy snow in the mountains could not be borne, and had written a letter and was about to send someone to welcome you; your coming now is truly a response to my feeling.” Yet in the end he released the host, and the sanctuary was preserved whole. He firmly kept me to pass the winter, questioning the Way morning and evening, and I spoke for him the Xuyan. At that time Lord Gao, the Regional Commander, had been moved to garrison Dai commandery, and hearing I was in the office, he said to Lord Hu: “My family has a garden pavilion with many inscriptions and poems; I would seek one poem from a man of high attainment.” Lord Hu agreed, and spoke to me of it. I said: “There is not a single character in my breast; how can I make a poem?” and firmly refused. Lord Gao pressed again and again, and Lord Hu had no way out and begged me hard; so he took collections of ancient and modern poems and set them on the desk to stir my thoughts. I happened to open one, and while I was framing a thought, suddenly the mechanism stirred, and phrases came swift and fast, not to be held back. When Lord Hu came back from the hall, I had already set down twenty or thirty pieces. I suddenly became aware and said: “This is the demon of literary habit,” and at once stopped, taking only one piece to put off the matter, not daring to send out the rest. Yet the mechanism could not be stopped, and before I knew it all the poetry, books, and rhapsodies I had studied before, every one that had ever entered my eyes, appeared at once before me and filled the whole of space, so that even if my whole body were a mouth I could not utter it, and I no longer knew what my own body and mind were. Silently I looked at myself, in a state as if about to fly up, and there was nothing to be done. The next day, after Lord Hu had seen Lord Gao off, I thought alone: “This is exactly what Chan Master Faguang called the Chan illness. Now that I am in the midst of it, who can cure it for me? There is no other way; only sleep can dissolve it. If I can sleep peacefully, that will be my good fortune.” So I shut the door and forced myself to lie down. At first I could not at all; after a long while, I suddenly sat forgetting, as in sleep; the boy knocked at the door and it did not open, and when he pounded on it there was no answer. Lord Hu returned and urgently asked after me; learning this, he had the window broken and entered, and saw me sitting upright wrapped in my robe, and called me with no answer, and shook me without moving me. Earlier, in the study, a Buddha had been enshrined, and on the offering table there was a small bell. Lord Hu picked it up and asked: “What is this used for?” I had said: “When a monk of the Western Regions enters concentration and cannot awake, one sounds this and he wakes — I once heard such a saying.” The Lord suddenly remembered it and said: “Has the Master entered concentration?” and quickly took the bell and sounded it at my ear several dozen times; then I gradually and faintly came to, and opening my eyes and looking around, did not know where my body was. The Lord said: “I went away, and the Master at once shut the door and sat; it is now five days. How is it with you?” I said: “I do not know; it was only one breath.” When I had spoken, I sat silent and examined closely, and in the end did not know what place this was, nor how I had entered it. Then I looked back on the mountain, and on all my former pilgrimage, and each thing was a matter of dream, sought and not found. And all that former clamor that filled the sky was like rain scattered and clouds gathered up, the vast sky as if washed, all still and without a trace of image. Mind empty and environment still, its joy beyond all comparison. Then I said: “When stillness is utmost, light penetrates; / In still illumination, the void is contained. / Turning back to look upon the world, / It is like a matter in a dream” — the Buddha’s words truly did not deceive me. I planned to return to the mountain at the new year, and so told Lord Hu that the forests of Mt. Tai were being bitterly cut by wicked merchants, and that the bodhisattva’s sanctuary would soon be bare and without a blade of grass. The Lord prepared a memorial requesting a strict prohibition. After that, when the state built and repaired the various monasteries, they all relied on this protected timber; otherwise there would have been no wood to take. (One meeting with Master Lianchi; second meetings with Lord Hu Shun’an and Dafang; one meeting each with Master Chekong and Lord Gao, the Regional Commander.)

Zheng has heard that the First Patriarch sealed the mind with the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra, and now the Patriarch Hanshan sealed the mind with the whole of the Śūraṅgama; the sage before and the sage after, their measure is one. Master Lianchi was a man of Renhe in Hangzhou, of the Shen clan, a great family, and a noted scholar of the county school. At thirty-two he went to the Venerable Tianli and had his head shaved, receiving the Dharma-name Zhuhong and the style Fohui. He then received full ordination from the Vinaya Master Wuchen Yu. Because the mourning for his mother was not yet ended, he carried her wooden tablet with him as he traveled, and wherever he dwelt he made offering, and at every meal he made offering. He visited teachers everywhere: going north to Wutai, he moved Mañjuśrī to emit light; reaching Funiu, he trained in the demon-marrow with the assembly; entering the capital, he consulted the two great elders Bianrong and Xiaoyan, and from both received opening. Passing through Dongchang, he suddenly had an awakening and made a verse: “The matter of twenty years ago was doubtful; / Three thousand li away, what strange encounter. / Burning incense, casting spears — all a dream; / Demon and Buddha strive in vain over right and wrong.” Returning south, he sat five Chan periods, and to the end never knew the name of the man on the neighbouring seat. In xīnwèi of Longqing he begged food at Fancun, and gradually brought the excellent karmic occasion of Yunqi to fulfillment, opening wide the one gate of the Pure Land and embracing all three capacities to the end. His works are the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra and Admonitions to Advance Through the Chan Gate; the Patriarch Hanshan praised these two works as revealing the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land, both issuing from the one mind, and as exceedingly subtle in their power to transform. From his leaving the world to its end there was nothing at all to criticize; he may be called one who in the Dharma-gate attained the Buddha’s whole substance and great function. In dīngsì, when I traveled east, I carried a text from Nanyue to make sacrifice, and complying with the request of his black- and white-robed disciples, composed his stupa-inscription, and also wrote seven portrait praises. The disciples of Yunqi painted a portrait of the Patriarch and left it hanging in the mountains, and he himself made a praise for it — all this was because of the karmic occasion of that one night’s heart-to-heart talk when he visited Mt. Tai in bǐngzǐ. Master Chekong first dwelt at Huanglong Pool on Mount Kuang; this time he came to dwell with me at the Dragon Gate, from the tenth month of winter to the fourth month of spring, when he returned to Mount Kuang, lodging at Mt. Tai for more than half a year. This was because the Patriarch was kept by Lord Hu of Yanping, and Master Che acted for him in the affairs about the cooking-pot. Earlier I heard that the false accusation of Dafang was just the doing of the wicked timber merchants who cut wood in the mountains, and that the various mountain communities begged the Patriarch to go and settle it with Lord Hu. Thus he began by settling Dafang’s difficulty and ended by prohibiting the cutting of Mt. Tai’s timber, and for a time all the mountain communities were moved by it — truly the non-duality of worldly dharma and Buddha-dharma. The Xuyan spoken in Lord Hu’s hall was set down from the mouth and from the hand, and was completed in a full month. Lord Hu had men record it into fascicles and at once gave it to the printer, asking that it be named Xuyan and sent out; it was in truth his first work. Its structure of chapters and sentences somewhat imitates the Laozi, but its cardinal purport is that the three teachings are one. Fourteen years later, at Mt. Lao, he wrote the Essay on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, so that the earlier and later works mutually illumine each other. I respectfully record three passages of the Xuyan to give an example of the rest. It says: He who is dense in affairs is sparse in mind; he who is dense in mind is penetrating in affairs. Hence the denser the affairs, the sparser the mind; the denser the mind, the more penetrating the affairs. One whose mind is not washed can have no way to be dense — this is why the sage values washing the mind and withdrawing to hide in the secret. It also says: The eye contains heaven and earth, yet a speck of dust can rob it of its clarity. The mind embraces the great void, yet a single thought can block its vastness. From this one knows that a single thought is the root of birth and death and the source of calamity and disaster; hence knowing the subtle and knowing the incipient, the sage keeps his guard. It also says: When a thought exists, things exist; when the mind is empty, dharmas are empty. Therefore if a thought is melted away, one is at ease in every karmic occasion; if the mind is like a round mirror, coming and going are ever at leisure. One who excels in this does not go beyond the ordinary, yet sits securely in the wondrous realm. Indeed the way of letters and the way of Chan are always one way; the demon of letters and the demon of Chan are always one demon. When the Way is a thousand feet high, the demon is a thousand feet high. Hence it is said: when the demon comes and the Buddha comes, if the Chan illness has not gone, then flying up or sitting in forgetting — how can one enter concentration? Do those in this world who style themselves men of Chan concentration understand this case of the small bell? Hu Shun’an, deep in karmic bond and earnest in feeling, for no reason stirred and asked about the small bell, and in the turning of an eye the subtle omen was fulfilled — how could this be anything a man can contrive? When I attended at the Zongjing Hall, what I saw morning and evening was this: when he sat, his legs were crossed; when he closed his eyes he entered concentration, when he opened them he came out of it; his two eyes would open like lightning, and he would answer a thousand words like an echo. That five-day concentration of his seems now no more than the affair of first entering the gate.
